guideline_source: Stanford Classification + ESC Aortic Diseases Guidelines
description: Aortic dissection is a life-threatening condition where a tear in the aortic intima allows blood to enter the aortic wall. Stanford Type A (involves ascending aorta) requires emergent surgery; Type B (descending only) is typically managed medically.

criteria.name: Ascending aorta involvement
criteria.definition: Dissection flap in ascending aorta on CTA or TEE

decision_rules.evidence_text: Type A dissection has 50% mortality at 48 hours without surgery. Emergency surgical repair is the definitive treatment.

decision_rules.rule_name: Type B Dissection - Descending aorta only

criteria.name: Descending aorta only
criteria.definition: Dissection begins distal to left subclavian, no ascending involvement

action.rationale: Most Type B managed medically unless complicated

decision_rules.evidence_text: Uncomplicated Type B dissection has 30-day mortality of 10% with medical therapy. Complicated cases (malperfusion, rupture) require intervention.

decision_rules.description: Sudden severe tearing or ripping chest/back pain

criteria.name: Tearing pain
criteria.character: Abrupt onset, maximal at onset, tearing quality

decision_rules.evidence_text: Sudden onset of pain (97%), severe intensity (90%), and tearing/ripping quality (51%) are characteristic. Pain maximal at onset (unlike MI which crescendos).

decision_rules.description: Pain that migrates from chest to back or abdomen

criteria.name: Migratory pain
keywords: started in chest went to back

decision_rules.evidence_text: Migratory pain reflects propagation of the dissection flap. Present in ~17% of patients but highly specific when present.
BP differential > 20 mmHg suggests branch vessel involvement by dissection flap. Present in 19% of Type A and 9% of Type B dissections.

decision_rules.description: New diastolic murmur suggesting aortic insufficiency
decision_rules.evidence_text: Aortic regurgitation in Type A dissection (40-75%) results from aortic root dilation or flap prolapse. May cause acute heart failure.

decision_rules.description: End-organ ischemia from dissection flap obstruction

action.rationale: Organ at risk of irreversible damage

decision_rules.evidence_text: Malperfusion occurs when dissection flap compromises branch vessel flow. Mesenteric malperfusion mortality >50%. Requires prompt intervention.

aortic_dissection_detection_score.description: ADD-RS helps identify patients at risk for aortic dissection

components.category: High-risk pain features (1 point if any)
items: Chest, back, or abdominal pain that is: abrupt onset, severe intensity, ripping/tearing

components.category: High-risk exam findings (1 point if any)
items: Perfusion deficit (pulse deficit, SBP differential, focal neuro deficit)

interpretation.1: Intermediate risk - D-dimer to screen (if < 500, very low probability)
interpretation.2-3: High risk - proceed directly to imaging (CTA or TEE)

clarifying_questions.question: Did the pain start suddenly and reach maximum intensity immediately?
clarifying_questions.question_zh: 疼痛是突然开始并立即达到最剧烈程度的吗？

clarifying_questions.question: Is the pain tearing, ripping, or knife-like in quality?
clarifying_questions.question_zh: 疼痛是撕裂样、刀割样的吗？

clarifying_questions.question: Has the pain moved from the chest to the back or abdomen?
clarifying_questions.question_zh: 疼痛是否从胸部转移到了背部或腹部？

clarifying_questions.question: Do you have a history of high blood pressure, connective tissue disease, or known aortic problems?
clarifying_questions.question_zh: 您有高血压、结缔组织病或已知的主动脉问题吗？

clarifying_questions.question: Is there any weakness in arms or legs, or any numbness?
clarifying_questions.question_zh: 手臂或腿有无力或麻木吗？

text_chunks.title: Stanford Classification of Aortic Dissection
text_chunks.content: Stanford classification divides aortic dissection based on involvement of ascending aorta: Type A - Involves ascending aorta (regardless of origin), requires EMERGENT SURGERY. Mortality 1-2% per hour without surgery, 50% at 48 hours. Type B - Limited to descending aorta (distal to left subclavian), usually managed MEDICALLY with BP and heart rate control. Complicated Type B (malperfusion, rupture, rapid expansion) requires intervention.

text_chunks.title: Aortic Dissection Red Flags
text_chunks.content: Red flags for aortic dissection: (1) Sudden severe chest/back pain maximal at onset, (2) Tearing or ripping quality, (3) Migratory pain, (4) Blood pressure differential > 20 mmHg between arms, (5) Pulse deficit, (6) New aortic regurgitation murmur, (7) Neurological symptoms (stroke), (8) Limb ischemia, (9) Marfan habitus or known connective tissue disease, (10) Widened mediastinum on CXR. Any red flag with compatible symptoms warrants urgent CTA.

text_chunks.title: Aortic Dissection Overview
text_chunks.content: Aortic dissection occurs when an intimal tear allows blood to enter the aortic media, creating a false lumen. Risk factors: hypertension (72%), atherosclerosis, Marfan syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve, prior aortic surgery, trauma, cocaine use. Peak incidence age 50-70. Male predominance 2:1. Presenting symptoms: chest pain (79%), back pain (53%), abdominal pain (30%). Classic triad of tearing pain, pulse deficit, widened mediastinum present in < 50%.

text_chunks.title: Dissection vs ACS vs PE
text_chunks.content: Differentiating aortic dissection from MI and PE: Dissection: sudden maximal pain at onset, tearing quality, migratory, BP differential, pulse deficit. MI: crescendo pain over minutes, pressure quality, ST changes, troponin elevation, no pulse deficit. PE: dyspnea predominant, pleuritic pain, hypoxia, leg swelling, positive Wells criteria. Key point: dissection pain is maximal AT ONSET, MI pain builds gradually. D-dimer elevated in both dissection and PE. If dissection suspected, get CTA, not just D-dimer.

text_chunks.title: Aortic Dissection Management
text_chunks.content: Initial management of suspected dissection: (1) Large-bore IV access x 2, (2) Continuous BP and cardiac monitoring, (3) Pain control - morphine to reduce sympathetic drive, (4) HR control - IV beta-blocker (esmolol or labetalol) to target HR < 60, (5) BP control after HR controlled - target SBP 100-120, (6) CTA aorta from arch to iliacs (or TEE if unstable), (7) Type O blood available, (8) Surgical consultation for Type A, (9) Avoid anticoagulation until diagnosis clarified. For Type A: emergent surgical repair. For uncomplicated Type B: medical management in ICU.
